title: Mock 3 · Numbers in Action
blurb: Liquidity and DuPont ratios, rights and dividend-discount maths, EV-to-price bridges, plus regulators and indicator basics.

questions.q: A Qualified Institutions Placement (QIP) is an issue of securities by a listed company made only to:
options: Existing shareholders in proportion to holdings
questions.explanation: A QIP is a private placement by a listed company exclusively to QIBs (mutual funds, banks, insurers, FPIs and similar institutions).
hints: Retail investors are not eligible in a QIP.
Allotment to specific persons such as promoters is a preferential issue.

questions.q: Which statement about a zero-coupon bond is correct?
options: It pays a higher coupon than other bonds
Its coupon resets every six months
It is issued at a discount and pays no periodic interest
questions.explanation: A zero-coupon bond pays no coupons; it is issued below face value and redeemed at face value, the difference being the investor's return. Its duration equals its maturity.
hints: It pays no coupon at all.

questions.q: Behavioural finance as an approach to equity research focuses on:
options: Statistical models built on large datasets
How psychological biases of investors can push prices away from fundamental value
questions.explanation: Behavioural finance studies how biases such as overconfidence, herding, anchoring and loss aversion affect investor decisions and market prices.

questions.q: Under the expenditure approach, GDP equals:
questions.explanation: Expenditure approach: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). The income approach sums factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit).
hints: GVA less depreciation is a net measure, not the expenditure formula.

questions.q: An industry showing rapidly rising sales, increasing profitability and new competitors entering is most likely in which life-cycle stage?
questions.explanation: The growth stage features fast demand growth, improving margins and entry of competitors. Pioneering is the early, uncertain stage; maturity has slower growth and consolidation; decline has shrinking demand.
hints: Pioneering has low sales and uncertain profits.
Maturity has slowing growth and stable competition.

questions.q: Which pair of KPIs is most relevant when analysing a private-sector bank?
options: Capacity utilisation and realisation per tonne
Average revenue per user and churn
Net interest margin and gross NPA ratio
questions.explanation: Banks are judged on profitability of lending (NIM) and asset quality (GNPA/NNPA), along with CASA ratio and capital adequacy.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of a competitive advantage based on network effects?
options: A payments app that becomes more useful as more users and merchants join it
A cement plant located next to a limestone mine
A drug company holding a patent
A retailer buying in bulk at lower cost
questions.explanation: Network effects arise when each additional user increases the value of the product for others, as in payments, marketplaces and social platforms.

questions.q: A company has current assets of ₹800 crore (including inventory of ₹300 crore) and current liabilities of ₹400 crore. Its quick ratio is:
questions.explanation: Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (800 - 300) / 400 = 1.25.
hints: 2.0 is the current ratio (inventory not excluded).

questions.q: A company has a net profit margin of 8%, asset turnover of 1.5 times and an equity multiplier (assets/equity) of 2. Its ROE is:
questions.explanation: DuPont: ROE = 8% x 1.5 x 2 = 24%.
hints: This adds the components instead of multiplying.
This is ROA (8% x 1.5), ignoring leverage.
This uses margin x equity multiplier only.

questions.q: Which pattern in a company's financials should most concern an analyst about earnings quality?
options: Rising PAT with rising operating cash flow
Dividend growing in line with profits
Reported PAT rising every year while cash flow from operations stays negative
questions.explanation: Profits that never turn into operating cash suggest aggressive revenue recognition or working-capital build-up - a classic earnings-quality red flag.
hints: Profit backed by cash is healthy.
This is a normal, healthy pattern.
Correct - profits without cash are suspect.

questions.q: A share trades at ₹300. The company announces a rights issue of 1 share for every 5 held at ₹240. The theoretical ex-rights price (TERP) is:
hints: This is the simple average of 300 and 240.
The price must fall because new shares are issued at a discount.

questions.q: A company is expected to pay a dividend of ₹6 next year. Dividends are expected to grow at 8% forever and the cost of equity is 13%. The value per share using the constant-growth dividend discount model is:
An analyst values a company's enterprise value at ₹8,000 crore. Debt is ₹1,500 crore, cash ₹500 crore and there are 50 crore shares. The equity value per share is:
questions.explanation: Equity value = EV - debt + cash = 8,000 - 1,500 + 500 = ₹7,000 crore; per share = 7,000 / 50 = ₹140.
hints: This subtracts debt but forgets to add cash.
This adds debt and subtracts cash - reversed.

questions.q: Transaction multiples (from past M&A deals) are usually higher than trading multiples of listed peers because they:
options: Are calculated on forward earnings only
Include a control premium paid by the acquirer
questions.explanation: Acquirers pay a premium for control and expected synergies, so deal multiples typically exceed the multiples at which minority stakes trade.
hints: They can be on historical or forward numbers.
SEBI does not set valuation multiples.

questions.q: A strengthening of the US Dollar Index generally tends to:
options: Put downward pressure on dollar-denominated commodity prices
Push global crude and gold prices sharply higher
Have no relationship with commodity prices
questions.explanation: Most commodities are priced in dollars. A stronger dollar makes them costlier for non-US buyers, reducing demand and typically pressuring dollar prices.
hints: A stronger dollar makes commodities dearer for non-US buyers, reducing demand.

questions.q: An investor buys a share at ₹250, receives a dividend of ₹5 and sells it after a year at ₹280. The holding-period return is:
hints: This is only the dividend yield.
Wrong denominator - HPR divides by the purchase price (₹250).

questions.q: A stock has a beta of 0.6. This means it is expected to:
options: Move in the opposite direction to the market
Be 60% more volatile than the market
Move about 0.6% for every 1% move in the market
questions.explanation: Beta measures sensitivity to the market. A beta of 0.6 implies the stock moves about 60% as much as the market, i.e., it is less volatile (defensive).
hints: Only a negative beta implies opposite movement.
Zero beta would mean no systematic risk.

questions.q: Where a research analyst has assigned a rating or price target to a stock for at least one year, the research report should include a daily closing-price graph covering:
options: The period of the rating or three years, whichever is shorter
The period since the company's IPO
questions.explanation: The RA Regulations require a daily closing price graph for the period for which the rating/price target has been assigned or three years, whichever is shorter.

questions.q: SEBI was given statutory powers to protect investors and regulate the securities market under:
questions.explanation: The SEBI Act, 1992 established SEBI as a statutory body with the mandate to protect investors' interests and to develop and regulate the securities market.
hints: SCRA regulates exchanges and contracts but predates SEBI.
The Companies Act governs companies, administered by MCA.

questions.q: A research analyst must disclose in its report if it or its associates hold actual or beneficial ownership in the subject company of at least:
options: 5% at the end of the quarter
0.5% on the date of the report
1% at the end of the month immediately preceding the report
questions.explanation: The RA Regulations require disclosure of actual/beneficial ownership of 1% or more of the subject company's securities at the end of the month immediately preceding publication.

questions.q: The National Pension System (NPS) is regulated by:
questions.explanation: PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority) regulates NPS and pension funds. IRDAI regulates insurance.
hints: RBI regulates banks and money markets.

questions.q: In Dow Theory, a secondary trend (correction within the primary trend) typically lasts about:
questions.explanation: Secondary trends are intermediate corrections lasting roughly three weeks to three months; primary trends last a year or more; minor trends under three weeks.

questions.q: The MACD line is calculated as:
questions.explanation: MACD = 12-period EMA - 26-period EMA; the signal line is a 9-period EMA of MACD.
hints: Those averages are used for golden/death crosses.
The 9-period EMA is the signal line of MACD, not MACD itself.
That is the upper Bollinger Band.

questions.q: When Bollinger Bands contract sharply and come close together, it usually indicates:
options: A period of low volatility that may precede a big move
questions.explanation: Narrow bands (a 'squeeze') reflect low volatility; volatility tends to expand afterwards, often with a sharp move in either direction.
hints: Band width says nothing about trend direction.
Overbought is judged by price at the upper band or oscillators.
Bands measure price volatility, not volume.

questions.q: A 'hammer' candlestick appearing after a prolonged fall in prices is generally considered:
options: A sign of a head-and-shoulders top
questions.explanation: A hammer has a small body and a long lower shadow, showing sellers pushed prices down but buyers pulled them back - a potential bullish reversal after a downtrend (needs confirmation).
hints: It suggests the selling is being absorbed.
A gap is not required for a hammer.
H&S tops form after uptrends, not falls.
